title: Responsible Regulation of Artificial Intelligence in the Legal Profession Through a Split Bar: Implications for Legal Educators
pub: Washington University Journal of Law & Policy, vol. 79, p. 167 (2026)
author: S.I. Strong

dom.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s concern that AI exposure and apparent performance do not establish independent judgment, but redirects the response toward an AI-free shared academic phase and a structurally differentiated profession in which solicitors and barristers may rely on AI differently. This is materially more restrictive and institutionally prescriptive than the cluster’s conditional, supervised-integration framing.
qs: Disallowing the use of generative AI during the academic phase of legal education not only promotes actual (as opposed to apparent) learning and fosters a common understanding between post-AI solicitors and barristers about the content of the law, but it is consistent with rules of professional responsibility outlining lawyers' ethical duties to personally verify the output of generative AI.

England has used a split bar for centuries, and adapting that model to allow different branches of the profession to utilize generative AI in different ways and for different purposes promotes public confidence in the judicial system while also benefitting clients, students, and individual lawyers.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source shares the cluster’s concern that AI reliance may weaken legal expertise and the capacity to verify outputs, but it does not analyze the law-firm pyramid, leverage, junior-generated revenue or buyer-driven restructuring. Instead, it reframes the response around professional bifurcation and an AI-free academic phase, offering a materially different regulatory and educational model.
qs: This Essay proposes a new way of structuring both the legal profession and legal education, building on time-tested techniques used in England while incorporating modifications that take the special nature of generative AI into account.

Disallowing the use of generative AI during the academic phase of legal education not only promotes actual (as opposed to apparent) learning and fosters a common understanding between post-AI solicitors and barristers about the content of the law, but it is consistent with rules of professional responsibility outlining lawyers' ethical duties to personally verify the output of generative AI.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Strong accepts that AI offers immediate time and cost gains while creating serious competence and deskilling risks, but rejects verification and incremental workflow safeguards as an adequate response. The source redirects the cluster’s practical framing toward fundamental professional and educational restructuring through an AI-adapted split bar that separates AI-reliant routine work from preserved human expertise.
qs: This Essay argues that the best—if not only—way to respond to empirically-established concerns relating to the use of generative AI is to adopt a split bar system, similar to what is used in England.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: The source does not directly assess whether junior pipelines face the sharpest workforce risk or whether broad lawyer displacement is occurring. Instead, it shifts the priority to cognitive and educational harms from generative AI and advocates urgent structural reform of legal practice and education, offering a constructive but materially different framing.
qs: This Essay proposes a new way of structuring both the legal profession and legal education, building on time-tested techniques used in England while incorporating modifications that take the special nature of generative AI into account.
According to numerous empirical studies, generative AI robs students of both their motivation and ability to learn complex legal concepts.

st.t: Professional governance: Existing duties need active AI scrutiny
st.an: Strong accepts responsible AI adoption and the need to protect human values, but argues that active scrutiny and incremental adjustment of existing professional systems are inadequate. She redirects the governance agenda toward fundamental reform of the legal profession and legal education, though the supplied abstract does not specify the proposed institutional design.
qs: Even a cursory analysis of the extent and nature of the dangers of generative AI suggests that simply tweaking existing systems will not be enough.
Instead, fundamental reforms of the legal profession and legal education are needed to ensure that adequate protections are in place.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: Strong accepts that AI should be controlled rather than autonomous and that lawyers must verify outputs, but argues that supervision and disclosure are structurally inadequate. The source redirects the cluster’s governance model toward an English-style split bar, differentiated AI-use permissions and AI-free foundational education to preserve independent expertise.
qs: This Essay argues that the best—if not only—way to respond to empirically-established concerns relating to the use of generative AI is to adopt a split bar system, similar to what is used in England.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source shares the cluster’s caution toward uncritical AI adoption, but redirects the analysis from selective, task-specific deployment and continuous risk-based governance toward urgent, comprehensive structural regulation, including a split-bar proposal. The supplied evidence asserts urgency and systemic reform without substantively engaging the cluster’s task-level capability, verification, workflow-redesign or empirical claims.
qs: Economic, social, and political forces are pressuring individuals and institutions to adopt pro-AI agendas, based in many cases on value-laden presumptions about the assumed benefits of technology rather than on fully informed analyses regarding the advantages and disadvantages of various strategies.
Instead, more comprehensive solutions, including the one proposed herein, must be considered, and must be considered in the near, not distant, future.

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: Strong accepts the need to develop independent legal judgment alongside AI competence and materially extends the staged-exposure approach into a structural model: a shared AI-restricted academic foundation followed by differentiated vocational paths. Its categorical claims about cognitive harm are stronger than the cluster’s evidence-cautious conclusions, but its overall prescription exemplifies and develops the timing-based reform position.
qs: Student use of generative AI would be limited or disallowed to ensure that students obtained an independent understanding of the material and honed their analytical skills through conventional means.
Those seeking to qualify as a post-AI solicitor would enroll in a one-year vocational course that focused heavily on how to use generative AI in legal settings.

kp.k: Cognitive harms motivate structural rather than incremental reform
kp.d: Strong argues that generative AI's central risks concern human cognition and justice-system functioning, not merely technical accuracy. She reports empirical research on impaired learning, reduced motivation and critical thinking, and warns of professional deskilling. The supplied essay does not provide study designs, sample sizes or quantitative results; its recommendation for urgent structural reform builds on these reported findings and projected harms.
qs: Indeed, empirical studies suggest that the most compelling and pervasive problem with AI—particularly generative AI—will be its negative effect on human behavior and cognition.
Indeed, experts have already voiced concerns about the loss of knowledge and abilities (a process known as deskilling) as generative AI becomes ever-more firmly entrenched in the justice sector.

kp.k: Disclosure and human verification are insufficient safeguards
kp.d: Strong asserts that voluntary disclosures and human checking have failed both operationally, through missed hallucinations and breaches of workplace AI bans, and conceptually, because they do not address cognitive deterioration or systemic effects. These are the author's grounds for moving beyond existing safeguards, rather than measured failure rates presented in the essay.
qs: So far, the primary means of addressing the challenges associated with generative AI have involved voluntary disclosures and human review of machine outputs.

Unfortunately, these techniques have not only failed on their own terms, with lawyers failing to catch, let alone disclose, hallucinations to courts and employees breaching their own firms' bans on generative AI, but they have also failed to address the real problem with generative AI, namely, the detrimental effect that generative AI has on individuals' cognitive skills and the operation of the justice system as a whole.

kp.k: An English-inspired split bar would allocate AI use
kp.d: Strong proposes two regulated professional branches, using the English barrister–solicitor distinction as an institutional analogy rather than adopting it unchanged. One branch would deliver standardized services with generative AI; the other would preserve independent human analysis of difficult legal questions. This is a proposed reorganization, not an observed market development.
qs: Instead, the proposal allocates different responsibilities to different branches of the legal profession based on their use of and facility with generative AI.

The current proposal resembles the English system by classifying one group of lawyers as providers of objective, independent legal advice concerning complex questions of law (similar to English barristers) and one group of lawyers as providers of more standardized legal advice and services (similar to English solicitors).

kp.k: Post-AI solicitors would automate standardized legal services
kp.d: The proposed solicitors would be clients' initial contact and use generative AI extensively in both transactional and litigation work within established legal boundaries. Strong grounds this allocation in her characterization of AI as suited to duplication rather than innovation, while retaining a need for legal acumen. She predicts time and cost savings rather than documenting realized outcomes.
qs: In the model proposed herein, the providers of standardized legal advice would rely heavily on generative AI to facilitate both their transactional and litigation-related tasks, since generative AI is best-suited for duplication rather than innovation.

While some legal acumen would be necessary to provide appropriate advice, generative AI would allow significant savings of time and costs in matters that fell within well-established legal boundaries.

kp.k: Post-AI barristers would reserve complex work for humans
kp.d: A smaller branch would address novel or complicated legal questions without generative AI, using human-generated research and analysis. Regulations would restrict its scope of work. Strong anticipates that complexity and the relatively small number of practitioners would support higher fees than those charged by post-AI solicitors.
qs: The second group of legal professionals would focus on novel or complicated questions of law that fell outside well-established legal boundaries.
These lawyers would not incorporate generative AI into their work, but would instead provide independent advice based on human—rather than machine—generated research and analysis.

Regulations would identify the limited types of matters that these lawyers could take on, but the more challenging nature of their work and relatively small number of individuals working in this field (as compared to post-AI solicitors) would allow them to charge higher fees for their services.

kp.k: Referrals and organizational separation would support specialization
kp.d: Solicitors would be encouraged, and sometimes required, to refer appropriate issues to barristers. Strong argues that distinct regulated responsibilities and issue-specific advice would preserve referral incentives without transferring whole matters. Organizational options include independent chambers, boutique-like partnerships or separate practice groups within mixed firms; she says some independent barristers would remain necessary under the mixed-firm option because of client-poaching concerns.
qs: However, post-AI solicitors would be encouraged (and in some cases required under the relevant regulations) to seek the assistance of post-AI barristers in appropriate matters.
A second possibility would see post-AI barristers working in the same firm as post-AI solicitors but housed in a different practice group.

Pragmatically, however, this approach would still need some post-AI barristers to work independently to facilitate the referral of novel questions of law, since concerns would arise about post-AI barristers poaching clients on behalf of their post-AI solicitor-partners.

kp.k: Shared foundational education would restrict generative AI
kp.d: Strong recommends a common academic law degree, preferably undergraduate to reduce educational costs, emphasizing substantive law over practical skills. Limiting or prohibiting student generative AI use would aim to develop independent understanding and analytical ability before specialization. She also links this foundation to lawyers' responsibility to personally verify AI output and to informed choice between the two career paths.
qs: It is recommended that the degree be offered at the undergraduate level, as is the case in England, to cut down on educational costs.
Student use of generative AI would be limited or disallowed to ensure that students obtained an independent understanding of the material and honed their analytical skills through conventional means.
Because the academic phase is identical for both branches of the profession, students have time to make an informed decision about which path is best for them.

kp.k: Vocational training would diverge by professional branch
kp.d: After the shared degree, aspiring solicitors would take a one-year vocational course focused on generative AI, potentially covering coding, AI research strategies and ethics. Barrister training would instead emphasize traditional research, analysis and drafting for novel questions with little or no AI assistance. Both routes would then require practical experience through traineeships or pupillages; the proposal does not specify their duration.
qs: Those seeking to qualify as a post-AI solicitor would enroll in a one-year vocational course that focused heavily on how to use generative AI in legal settings.
Vocational training for post-AI barristers would de-emphasize technology skills. Instead, these students would learn more traditional approaches to legal research, analysis, and drafting.
Both types of vocational courses would be followed by hands-on work experience. Post-AI solicitors would undertake traineeships while post-AI barristers would undertake pupillages.

kp.k: Transparency and judicial expertise are anticipated institutional benefits
kp.d: Strong predicts that explicit rules governing which lawyers may use AI would clarify the provenance of legal advice and increase public confidence. She further suggests judges would likely come from the barrister branch because independent research and critical analysis would be important for trial matters with novel elements. These are anticipated effects of the proposed system, not demonstrated outcomes.
qs: Clearly outlining which lawyers can rely on generative AI, and when they can rely on generative AI, allows both the profession and the public to understand when, how, and to what extent legal advice has been generated by a machine.
As a result, it appears likely that judges in the post-AI system would be initially trained as barristers, as is currently the case in England.

kp.k: Lower routine costs could improve access to justice
kp.d: Strong argues that AI's time and cost savings can increase access to justice. Under her model, automation and cheaper education would lower solicitor-side costs, while higher-priced barrister expertise would be purchased selectively. She asserts that this selective engagement would avoid systemic cost increases, without providing a quantified cost model.
qs: No one can doubt the ability of generative AI to reduce time and costs, which can subsequently increase access to justice.

Streamlining the educational path for post-AI solicitors (by allowing the academic phase of training to be completed at the undergraduate, rather than graduate, level) can also help keep costs down for clients.
However, costs would not increase on a systemic basis, since barristers would not be engaged in all matters.

kp.k: Career differentiation could accommodate work-life preferences
kp.d: Strong reports that many younger lawyers favor a traditional 9-to-5 schedule over the 80-hour weeks she associates with older partnership aspirants. Conditional on AI delivering promised time savings, she predicts the solicitor route could accommodate that preference, while the barrister route would attract those willing to undertake long hours and cognitively demanding work. This is an anticipated sorting mechanism, not evidence of observed working-hour reductions.
qs: Many young lawyers aspire to a more traditional 9-to-5 approach in their careers, rather than the 80-hour work weeks typical of older lawyers pursuing partnership.

If generative AI lives up to its promise of reducing time spent on various tasks, then those who want a more reasonable work-life balance will be able to obtain that by choosing a career as a post-AI solicitor.

kp.k: Weak incoming skills and institutional inertia threaten implementation
kp.d: Strong identifies two drawbacks: the model assumes foundational reading, writing and analytical skills that she fears earlier AI reliance will weaken, and status quo bias may obstruct institutional reform. She speculates that students could resist remedial instruction because of lost motivation or ability, citing reports of AI's addictive nature. The essay nevertheless calls for near-term comprehensive action rather than waiting or making small adjustments.
qs: First, the educational model is built on the assumption that students will arrive at law school with certain basic skills in reading, writing, and analysis.
This concern is particularly acute given reports about the addictive nature of generative AI.
This bias favoring current educational and professional structures may derail any efforts to respond reasonably to the challenges of generative AI.
This is not an issue that can wait, nor is it something that can be resolved through small adjustments to the existing system.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Strong argues that generative AI delivers efficiencies but threatens legal cognition, learning, and independent expertise; she proposes an AI-differentiated split bar to preserve those benefits while limiting harms.
pts.d: Strong makes the following claims and predictions. (1) Generative AI reduces the time and cost of legal work, potentially increasing access to justice, particularly for standardized matters within established legal boundaries. She characterizes it as better suited to duplication than innovation. (2) Its principal dangers concern human behavior and cognition, including diminished capacity to craft sophisticated legal arguments, harm to public perceptions of justice, and imminent professional deskilling. (3) Generative AI undermines students' motivation, critical thinking, and acquisition of complex material; its apparently addictive character may make reliance difficult to reverse. Earlier exposure may leave incoming law students with weaker reading, writing, and analytical skills and less willingness or ability to develop them. (4) Voluntary disclosures and human verification have failed to prevent problematic use and do not address the broader cognitive and systemic harms. (5) As a proposed response, rather than a description of an existing market division, Strong advocates 'post-AI solicitors' using generative AI heavily for standardized services and 'post-AI barristers' providing human-generated analysis for novel or complicated legal questions without generative AI. Solicitors would remain the initial client contact and refer appropriate issues to barristers, sometimes under mandatory referral rules. Strong predicts sufficient referral incentives because the branches would have different regulated functions and barristers could advise on a single issue rather than take over the matter. (6) She expects the scarcer, specialist barristers to charge higher fees, but argues that overall costs would not increase because their involvement would be limited to matters requiring heightened expertise; AI-supported services and shorter educational pathways would reduce other costs. (7) She predicts that clearly separating AI-assisted from human-generated advice would increase transparency and public confidence. Judges would likely be drawn from the barrister branch, bringing independent research and analytical expertise that would further increase confidence. (8) She proposes a shared, preferably undergraduate, academic law degree with generative AI limited or prohibited, followed by separate vocational training and work experience. This is intended to preserve independent understanding, support lawyers' personal verification of AI output, and allow informed career choices. (9) Conditional on AI delivering its promised time savings, the solicitor route could support more conventional working hours, while the barrister route would suit those seeking cognitively demanding work. (10) Strong argues that fundamental, urgent reform is needed rather than incremental adjustments; status quo bias may obstruct it.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Strong invokes empirical research, professional incidents, ethical duties, and the English split bar; the proposed system's outcomes are supported chiefly by institutional analogy and reasoning rather than reported tests of the proposal.
pts.d: For cognitive and educational harms, Strong repeatedly refers to empirical studies of students and knowledge workers, reports of addiction, and expert concerns about deskilling. The supplied text does not identify those studies, their populations, methods, effect sizes, or observation periods. Strong also refers to her other publications for fuller treatment of behavioral and systemic harms. For the inadequacy of disclosure and verification, she cites lawyers' failures to catch or disclose hallucinations and employees' violations of firm AI bans, without naming cases or supplying frequencies. These are reported incidents, not measured hallucination rates. Her educational argument also invokes professional-responsibility duties to personally verify AI output, without specifying a rule. The split-bar proposal draws on her account of English barrister and solicitor roles, training, and centuries of institutional experience; this historical analogy is not presented as a trial of an AI-differentiated bar. Predicted savings, higher specialist fees, referral incentives, confidence gains, and judicial benefits follow from her account of specialization, limited specialist involvement, transparency, and independent expertise; no quantified market model or outcome study is supplied. The work-life prediction is expressly conditional and rests partly on her account of younger lawyers' preferences. Resistance to reform is linked to empirical work on status quo bias, again without study details in the supplied text.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2026 essay presents some harms and control failures as already occurring, deskilling as imminent, and split-bar benefits as conditional future outcomes requiring near-term institutional reform.
pts.d: Strong locates the profession's response to generative AI from 2023 onward. She treats learning harms and failures of current safeguards as existing problems and describes additional professional deskilling as imminent; no numerical forecast horizon is supplied. She calls for comprehensive reform in the near rather than distant future. Efficiencies are most appropriate where legal boundaries are well established and reduced creativity poses relatively little risk; independent human analysis is reserved for novel or complex questions. Higher barrister fees, limited aggregate costs, transparent service categories, and referral incentives depend on implementing differentiated regulation and limiting specialist work to appropriate matters. The proposed employment structure remains open: barristers could work independently or in separate groups within mixed firms, but Strong says some independent provision would still be needed to avoid client-poaching concerns. Educational benefits depend on a shared substantive foundation with restricted AI use and separate subsequent training; she explicitly notes that this assumes students arrive with basic literacy and analytical skills. The work-life benefit is conditional on AI actually reducing task time. Judicial recruitment from the barrister branch is described as likely rather than certain, and status quo bias is identified as a possible obstacle to implementation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Strong's claims concern standardized and specialist legal providers, clients, students and educators, judges, regulators, and the public, with different exposure to AI and different projected benefits and risks.
pts.d: Providers of standardized transactional and litigation services would become AI-intensive, client-facing post-AI solicitors, offering potential time and cost savings while retaining enough legal understanding to advise appropriately and verify outputs. Providers of novel or complex legal analysis would become a smaller, higher-fee, non-generative-AI barrister branch tasked with preserving independent expertise. Firms could organize those branches separately or house them in distinct practice groups; independent specialists would support referrals without threatening referring firms' client relationships. Clients would initially approach solicitors and incur specialist fees only where needed, while gaining clearer information about whether advice is machine- or human-generated. The public could benefit through increased access to justice and confidence in adjudication; Strong separately warns that AI can harm public perceptions of justice. Students would share foundational education before choosing divergent vocational routes, potentially with reduced degree costs, but may arrive with AI-related deficits in basic skills and learning motivation. Legal educators would have to restructure curricula, restrict foundational AI use, and potentially address those deficits. Junior lawyers seeking conventional working hours could prefer the solicitor route, while those seeking intensive analytical engagement could pursue barrister work. Judges would likely be recruited from the independent-analysis branch. Professional regulators would define permissible work, AI use, and referral obligations.
